title: Geometric realization into k-spaces: adjunction, finite limits and simplex pairs
statement: Use simplicial sets, standard simplices, horns and geometric realization as defined in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]; define $\partial\Delta^n$ as the simplicial subset of monotone maps to $[n]$ whose image omits a vertex. A k-space is a topological space whose topology is final with respect to all continuous maps to it from compact Hausdorff spaces; write $\mathcal K$ for the category of k-spaces and continuous maps. This category has all small limits and colimits; colimits are topological colimits, and limits are obtained by applying the k-space topology to topological limits. Realization takes values in $\mathcal K$ and is left adjoint to the singular complex $\operatorname{Sing}(T)_n=\operatorname{Cont}(|\Delta^n|,T)$ with operators given by precomposition. It preserves all small colimits and all finite limits in $\mathcal K$, naturally in the diagrams. In particular $|X\times_ZY|\cong |X|\times_{|Z|}^{\mathcal K}|Y|$. For $n\geq0$, the realized pair $(|\Delta^n|,|\partial\Delta^n|)$ is homeomorphic to $(D^n,S^{n-1})$, with $D^0$ a point and $S^{-1}=\varnothing$. For $n\geq1$ and $0\leq i\leq n$, $(|\Delta^n|,|\Lambda_i^n|)$ is homeomorphic to $(D^{n-1}\times[0,1],D^{n-1}\times\{0\})$. Here $D^n$ is the closed Euclidean unit ball and $S^{n-1}$ its boundary.

proof.text: Define $kT$ by compact tests as in the statement. The identity $kT\to T$ is continuous, because every originally open set passes every test. Every original compact test $a:C\to T$ is still continuous into $kT$, directly from the definition of its open sets; conversely every map into $kT$ is continuous into $T$. Thus the compact tests of $kT$ and $T$ coincide, so $k(kT)=kT$. For a k-space $X$, a map $f:X\to T$ is continuous into $kT$ if it is continuous into $T$: for a k-open $U$ and each compact test $a:C\to X$, $(fa)^{-1}(U)$ is open, so $f^{-1}(U)$ is open by the k-space condition. The reverse implication follows from the continuous identity. This proves the universal mapping property of k-ification.

proof.text: For a small diagram of spaces, its topological limit is the subset of the product consisting of compatible tuples, with topology generated by inverse images of opens under the coordinate projections. A map into it is continuous exactly when its coordinate maps are continuous. Its topological colimit is the disjoint union of the underlying spaces modulo the identifications generated by diagram arrows, with the final topology for the structure maps; a map out is continuous exactly when its composites with the structure maps are continuous. These descriptions prove both universal properties. For a diagram of k-spaces, applying step 1 to the topological limit proves that its k-ification is the limit in $\mathcal K$. The topological colimit is already a k-space: if $U$ passes all compact tests to the colimit, its inverse image in each diagram object passes that object's tests and hence is open; the final topology makes $U$ open. This includes the empty diagram. In particular the terminal object is a point and products are k-ifications of ordinary products.

proof.text: By [lem-coef-standard-simplex-compact], every standard topological simplex is compact; it is Hausdorff because two different coordinate vectors have disjoint neighborhoods obtained by separating a differing real coordinate. Any compact Hausdorff space is a k-space, since its identity is one of its compact tests. A disjoint union of k-spaces is a k-space: test-open sets restrict to test-open, hence open, sets on every summand. A quotient of a k-space is a k-space: pull back a test-open set along its quotient map, use all compact tests on the source, and apply the quotient topology. The quotient construction in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones] therefore makes every realization a k-space. For a map $h:|X|\to T$, define $\eta_h(x)(t)=h([x,t])$ for $x\in X_n$. Its components are continuous, and the quotient relations give $\eta_h(X(\alpha)x)=\eta_h(x)\circ\alpha_*$. Conversely a simplicial map $\eta:X\to\operatorname{Sing}(T)$ defines $h([x,t])=\eta(x)(t)$; these same equations make it well-defined and the final quotient topology makes it continuous. These constructions are inverse and commute with pre- and postcomposition, proving the natural adjunction into $\mathcal K$.

proof.text: For a small simplicial diagram $X_j$ and a k-space $T$, step 3 identifies compatible continuous maps $|X_j|\to T$ with compatible simplicial maps $X_j\to\operatorname{Sing}(T)$. Their unique assembly is a map from the degreewise colimit $\operatorname{colim}_j X_j$ to $\operatorname{Sing}(T)$ (in each degree this is the disjoint-union quotient of sets). Step 3 turns it back into a unique map $|\operatorname{colim}_j X_j|\to T$ compatible with the original maps. Thus the canonical realization cocone is colimiting, naturally in the diagram; this proves preservation of all small colimits.

proof.text: For $\Delta^n$, send a representative $(\alpha:[r]\to[n],t)$ to the coordinate vector $\alpha_*t$. Its inverse sends $u$ to $[\mathrm{id}_{[n]},u]$. The quotient relation identifies the composites with the identity, and the coordinate sums and characteristic map make the two maps continuous. This gives the usual topological simplex. For $\Delta^m\times\Delta^n$, a simplex is a chain of vertices $(a,b)$ in the ordered lattice $[m]\times[n]$. It is nondegenerate exactly when its vertices are distinct: a repetition in the chain factors through a surjection, and distinctness prevents such a factorization. Consider the comparison map to the product of topological simplices. For $u=(u_0,\ldots,u_m)$ and $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_n)$, form the two lists of partial sums $\sum_{a=0}^i u_a$ and $\sum_{b=0}^j v_b$ (omit their final sums $1$), and sort their union together with $0,1$. For each interval between consecutive distinct cuts, choose its midpoint; it lies in unique positive coordinate blocks for $u$ and $v$, giving a lattice vertex $(a,b)$. The interval length is the weight of this vertex. The resulting strictly increasing chain and positive weights give a realization point mapping to $(u,v)$. Conversely the projections of any strictly increasing weighted chain recover these cuts and interval lengths: a cut occurs whenever either coordinate block changes. Therefore the normal-form uniqueness of [lem-cbc-realization-cw-subcomplex] proves this point is unique.

proof.text: Continuity of the inverse in step 5 does not require a Hausdorffness theorem for arbitrary realizations. Choose any shuffle order of the $m$ first-list cuts and $n$ second-list cuts. The region where that weak ordering holds is closed, as it is given by finitely many linear inequalities. There are finitely many shuffles and these regions cover the product of simplices. On each region insert repeated cuts and use their successive differences as nonnegative barycentric coordinates on its fixed maximal lattice path. This affine map followed by the corresponding characteristic map into $|\Delta^m\times\Delta^n|$ is continuous. Tied cuts have weight zero, and deleting those vertices gives the unique positive chain of step 5, so these maps agree on intersections. To verify the glued map is continuous, the inverse image of any closed set is a finite union of closed subsets of these closed regions, hence closed. The comparison is continuous by its defining coordinate projections. The ordinary product of the two simplices is compact Hausdorff: by [lem-coef-standard-simplex-compact] the simplex with coordinates indexed by pairs $(a,b)$ is compact. The continuous row-sum/column-sum map from it onto the product is surjective, since $(u,v)$ is the image of weights $w_{a,b}=u_av_b$. The image is compact directly by pulling back an open cover and then its finite subcover; coordinate neighborhoods separate unequal pairs. Thus it is already a k-space, and the homeomorphism also identifies the product in $\mathcal K$. The empty product is realized by $\Delta^0$, a point.

proof.text: Every simplicial set $X$ is the colimit of its standard simplices indexed by pairs $(n,x\in X_n)$ and operators carrying one simplex to another. This indexing category is small. Indeed compatible maps from these simplices to $Z$ are exactly a collection of elements $z_x\in Z_n$ satisfying $z_{X(\alpha)x}=Z(\alpha)z_x$; this is exactly a simplicial map $X\to Z$. The product of simplicial sets commutes with these colimits separately in each variable: degreewise a function on $(\operatorname{colim}_j A_j)\times B$ is exactly a compatible family of functions on $A_j\times B$, so it has the stated universal property. The product in $\mathcal K$ also commutes with small colimits separately. In fact [lem-coef-kspace-exponential-law] identifies maps $k(C\times Y)\to Z$ with maps $C\to kC(Y,Z)$; by the colimit universal property the latter are compatible families of maps $C_j\to kC(Y,Z)$, and uncurrying gives precisely a cocone of maps $k(C_j\times Y)\to Z$. Apply step 4 and these two universal properties first to the simplex presentation of $X$ and then to that of $Y$. The comparison $|X\times Y|\to|X|\times^{\mathcal K}|Y|$ is consequently the colimit, in each variable, of the homeomorphisms proved in step 6, and is a homeomorphism. For completeness, write $q_j:A_j\to B_j$ for any of these simplex comparison homeomorphisms, and $a:A_j\to A_{j'}$, $b:B_j\to B_{j'}$ for the maps induced by simplex operators. Both composites $q_{j'}a$ and $bq_j$ have the same two projections, hence are equal. Multiplying this equality by the inverses gives $a q_j^{-1}=q_{j'}^{-1}b$. If $i_j:A_j\to\operatorname{colim} A_j$ are the structure maps, the maps $i_jq_j^{-1}:B_j\to\operatorname{colim} A_j$ therefore form a compatible cocone and induce a continuous map from $\operatorname{colim} B_j$. Its composites with the comparison are identities after every structure map, hence are identities by the two colimit universal properties. Perform this construction in each of the two simplex indices. The comparisons commute with projections, so this proves natural preservation of finite products.

proof.text: Let $f,g:L\to M$ be simplicial maps and let $E_n=\{x\in L_n:f(x)=g(x)\}$ with its restricted operators. This is the degreewise equalizer. We prove that $|E|\hookrightarrow |L|$ has exactly the equalizer's underlying point set. By [lem-cbc-realization-cw-subcomplex], represent a point as $[x,t]$ with $x$ nondegenerate and every coordinate of $t$ positive. Write $f(x)=M(\alpha)a$ and $g(x)=M(\beta)b$ with $a,b$ nondegenerate and $\alpha,\beta$ increasing surjections, using [lem-weil-pbc-simplicial-set-nondegenerate-decomposition]. Their realization normal forms are $(a,\alpha_*t)$ and $(b,\beta_*t)$, with positive coordinates because each fiber is nonempty. If the realized values agree, uniqueness gives $a=b$ and $\alpha_*t=\beta_*t$. The partial sums of $t$ are strictly increasing. Each cut between consecutive fibers of an increasing surjection is therefore determined uniquely by the corresponding partial sum of its pushed-forward weights. Equal pushed-forward weights force identical fiber cuts, so $\alpha=\beta$ and $f(x)=g(x)$. Conversely every $x\in E$ certainly has equal realized images. Thus the equalizer subset is exactly the image of $|E|$, and [lem-cbc-realization-cw-subcomplex] gives it the ordinary subspace topology and shows it is closed.

proof.text: A closed subspace $A$ of a k-space $X$ is a k-space. If $B\subseteq A$ pulls back to a closed subset under every compact Hausdorff test to $A$, and $c:C\to X$ is a compact Hausdorff test, the set $c^{-1}(A)$ is closed in $C$, hence compact Hausdorff. The restricted map to $A$ makes $c^{-1}(B)$ closed in $c^{-1}(A)$ and therefore in $C$. The k-space criterion makes $B$ closed in $X$, hence in $A$. Applying this to step 8 shows the ordinary equalizer is already a k-space, so step 2 identifies it with the equalizer in $\mathcal K$. The homeomorphism respects its inclusion, proving realization preserves equalizers. Every finite diagram has its limit as the equalizer of the two maps $\prod_i X_i\rightrightarrows\prod_{a:i\to j}X_j$, sending a tuple respectively to $X(a)x_i$ and $x_j$. This formula has the limit universal property because equality is exactly compatibility of the tuple. Products and equalizers in simplicial sets are degreewise, and in $\mathcal K$ they are as above. Steps 7-8 consequently identify their comparison maps and prove natural preservation of every finite limit. A pullback is the equalizer in $X\times Y$ of its two maps to $Z$, giving the displayed pullback homeomorphism.

proof.text: Under step 5's standard-simplex identification, [lem-cbc-realization-cw-subcomplex] identifies the realization of each simplicial subset with its closed geometric subset. For the boundary this is the set where some coordinate vanishes. For the horn it is the set where $t_j=0$ for at least one $j\ne i$: the faces omitting a vertex other than $i$ are exactly its defining faces. A radial formula identifies the simplex and its boundary with a disk and sphere. For $n>0$, put $c=(1/(n+1),\ldots,1/(n+1))$ and $V=\{w:\sum_jw_j=0\}$. For a unit vector $w\in V$, define $\rho(w)=1/((n+1)\max_j(-w_j))$. The denominator is positive because a nonzero zero-sum vector has a negative coordinate; it is continuous and bounded away from zero: write $M=\max_j(-w_j)$. Some coordinate has absolute value at least $1/\sqrt{n+1}$ because $\sum_j w_j^2=1$. If that coordinate is negative then $M\geq1/\sqrt{n+1}$; if positive, the zero-sum relation forces one of the at most $n$ negative coordinates to have absolute value at least $1/(n\sqrt{n+1})$. Also $M\leq1$. These inequalities give uniform positive upper and lower bounds for $\rho$. The ray $c+rw$ lies in the simplex exactly for $0\leq r\leq\rho(w)$. Thus $rw\mapsto c+r\rho(w)w$, $0\leq r\leq1$, is a homeomorphism from the unit ball in $V$ to the simplex, with inverse obtained by dividing by $\rho(w)$. Continuity at the center follows from the bounded positive radial functions; continuity elsewhere follows from the displayed formulas. The affine space $V$, identifies isometrically with $\mathbb R^n$: the vectors $e_j-e_n$ for $0\leq j<n$ form a basis, and successive subtraction of projections and normalization (Gram--Schmidt) produces an orthonormal basis because no vector in this independent list becomes zero. Boundary points correspond precisely to $r=1$, proving the boundary pair. If $n=0$, the simplex is a point and its boundary is empty.

proof.text: For the horn pair, first take $n\geq2$ and let $F$ be the opposite face $t_i=0$, with barycenter $c_F$. Its horn subset $H$ is the cone from $e_i$ on $\partial F$: every point of $H$ except $e_i$ has the unique form $(1-s)e_i+sb$ with $b\in\partial F$, $0<s\leq1$. The map $(1-s)e_i+sb\mapsto c_F+s(b-c_F)$ is a homeomorphism $H\to F$, fixing their common boundary; its inverse uses the unique radial decomposition in $F$, whose continuity follows from the finite-coordinate radial formula of step 10. Send this $H$ to $F\times\{0\}$. Send the other part $F$ of the simplex boundary to the remaining boundary of $F\times[0,1]$ as follows. In the same radial coordinates $c_F+r(b-c_F)$, send $0\leq r\leq1/2$ to $(c_F+2r(b-c_F),1)$ and $1/2\leq r\leq1$ to $(b,2-2r)$. The formulas agree at $r=1/2$, are continuous at the center, and have continuous inverses given by halving the radial coordinate on the top and by $r=1-h/2$ on the side of height $h$. At $r=1$ this is $(b,0)$, so it agrees with the map from $H$. This is a homeomorphism of boundaries carrying $H$ to the bottom face. Let $\psi:\partial|\Delta^n|\to\partial(F\times[0,1])$ be this boundary homeomorphism and let $c,d$ be the respective interior barycenters. Every point other than $c$ has a unique expression $c+r(p-c)$ with $p\in\partial|\Delta^n|$ and $0<r\leq1$. Define the extension by $c\mapsto d$ and $c+r(p-c)\mapsto d+r(\psi(p)-d)$. Define its inverse by $d\mapsto c$ and $d+r(q-d)\mapsto c+r(\psi^{-1}(q)-c)$. Unique ray decompositions show that these maps are inverse and restrict to $\psi$ and $\psi^{-1}$. For both the simplex and $F\times[0,1]$, the distance to the boundary in a unit direction is the minimum of the finitely many positive facet-intersection distances; equivalently its reciprocal is the maximum of the finitely many normalized outward linear facet values and zero. The reciprocal is continuous, positive, and uniformly bounded above and below: the interior barycenter has a positive distance from each of finitely many facets, and both bodies have bounded coordinate ranges. Thus the radial lengths have uniform finite positive bounds. The ray formulas make the extension and its inverse continuous away from their centers; the uniform bounds prove continuity at the centers. This gives a homeomorphism $(|\Delta^n|,H)\cong(F\times[0,1],F\times\{0\})$. Apply step 10 to the $(n-1)$-simplex $F$ to obtain the required disk-cylinder pair. If $n=1$, the horn is the single vertex $e_i$, and the coordinate $t_{1-i}$ identifies the pair with $([0,1],\{0\})$. This covers every horn index, including both outer horns.
